sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark.

questions.q: (a) Write the IUPAC name of K[Ag(CN)2]. (b) Write the oxidation state of silver in it.
State true or false: (a) [Fe(CN)6]^3− is paramagnetic. (b) Transition metal ions in complexes are usually coloured.
questions.answer: (a) True (one unpaired electron). (b) True – due to d–d transitions.

questions.q: Name the type of isomerism in (a) [Co(NH3)5NO2]^2+ and [Co(NH3)5ONO]^2+ (b) [Co(NH3)6][Cr(C2O4)3] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(C2O4)3].
Fill in: (a) The hybridisation of Ni in [Ni(CN)4]^2− is ______. (b) The geometry of [NiCl4]^2− is ______.
Match: (a) EDTA (b) cis-platin (c) Haemoglobin with (i) Fe (ii) cancer therapy (iii) hexadentate ligand.
Identify (a) the ligands and (b) the counter ion in [Co(NH3)6]Cl3.
Write (a) the coordination number and (b) the oxidation state of Co in [Co(en)3]^3+.
State (a) the type of ligand SCN− and (b) the donor atoms.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of [PtCl6]^2− and K[Ag(CN)2].
What is meant by linkage isomerism? Give an example.
questions.answer: Isomerism due to ambidentate ligands that can attach through different donor atoms. [Co(NH3)5NO2]^2+ (N-bonded nitro) and [Co(NH3)5ONO]^2+ (O-bonded nitrito).

questions.q: What are outer-orbital and inner-orbital complexes? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Outer-orbital: octahedral complex using sp³d² (nd orbitals), high spin, e.g. [FeF6]^3−. Inner-orbital: uses d²sp³ ((n−1)d orbitals), low spin, e.g. [Fe(CN)6]^3−.

questions.q: Why is a solution of [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ green while [Ni(CN)4]^2− is colourless?
questions.answer: In [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ (Ni^2+, d⁸) two unpaired electrons undergo d–d transitions absorbing visible light. In [Ni(CN)4]^2− the strong-field CN− pairs all electrons (dsp², square planar, diamagnetic), so there is no d–d absorption in the visible region.

questions.q: Why is [Fe(CN)6]^3− paramagnetic?
questions.answer: Fe^3+ is d⁵; with strong CN− ligands the electrons pair up to d²sp³, leaving one unpaired electron.

questions.q: What is a chelate? Give an example.
questions.answer: A complex in which a polydentate ligand binds the metal through two or more donor atoms forming a ring, such as [Co(en)3]^3+ or the EDTA complex of Ca^2+.

questions.q: Define coordination number and give an example.
questions.answer: The number of donor atoms bonded to the central metal in a complex; it is 6 in [Co(NH3)6]^3+.

questions.q: Name the complex [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 and state its coordination number.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: For the complex [CoCl2(en)2]+: (a) how many geometrical isomers exist? (b) Is optical isomerism possible?
questions.answer:
(a) Two geometrical isomers: cis (Cl groups adjacent) and trans (Cl groups opposite).
(b) The cis form lacks a plane of symmetry and exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (d and l); the trans form is optically inactive. So three stereoisomers exist.

questions.q: Write the isomers of [Co(NH3)6][Cr(C2O4)3] and the type of isomerism shown.
questions.answer: [Cr(NH3)6][Co(C2O4)3] is the isomer, formed by exchange of the metals between cation and anion. This is coordination isomerism.

questions.q: Explain the bonding in [Fe(CN)6]^4− and [FeF6]^3− on the basis of valence bond theory.
questions.answer: [Fe(CN)6]^4−: Fe^2+ is d⁶; strong CN− pairs the electrons, using two 3d, one 4s and three 4p orbitals (d²sp³), diamagnetic, inner orbital. [FeF6]^3−: Fe^3+ d⁵; weak F− does not pair them, using 4s, 4p and two 4d (sp³d²), five unpaired electrons, outer orbital, paramagnetic.

questions.q: Explain crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes and the difference between high spin and low spin.
questions.answer: In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into t2g (lower) and eg (higher). If Δo is greater than the pairing energy (strong-field ligand), electrons pair up in t2g (low spin); if Δo is smaller (weak-field ligand), electrons occupy eg before pairing (high spin).

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names and the oxidation states of the metals in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl, K4[Fe(CN)6] and [Ni(CO)4].
State three applications of coordination compounds.
questions.answer: EDTA is used to estimate Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ (hardness) and in lead poisoning; cis-platin is an anticancer drug; extraction of silver and gold by cyanide complexes; haemoglobin, chlorophyll and vitamin B12 are coordination compounds.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: (a) Give the IUPAC names of (i) [PtCl6]^2− (ii) K[Ag(CN)2]. (b) For [CoCl2(en)2]+ (i) identify the number of geometrical isomers and draw their structures; (ii) state whether optical isomers exist.
questions.answer:
(a) (i) Hexachloridoplatinate(IV); (ii) potassium dicyanidoargentate(I).
(b) (i) Two: cis – the two Cl on adjacent corners of the octahedron with the two en rings spanning the remaining positions; trans – the two Cl on opposite corners (axial) with both en rings in the plane. (ii) The cis isomer has no plane of symmetry and shows optical isomerism (d and l forms); the trans isomer is optically inactive.

questions.q: (a) Write the isomers of [Co(NH3)6][Cr(C2O4)3] and name the type of isomerism. (b) A solution of [Ni(H2O)6]^2+ is green but a solution of [Ni(CN)4]^2− is colourless. Explain (Ni = 28).
questions.answer:
(a) [Cr(NH3)6][Co(C2O4)3]; coordination isomerism (the ligands are distributed differently between the cationic and anionic parts).
(b) Ni^2+ is 3d⁸. In [Ni(H2O)6]^2+, H2O is a weak ligand, so two unpaired electrons remain, sp³d² (outer), and d–d transitions give green colour. In [Ni(CN)4]^2−, CN− is a strong ligand which pairs the electrons, dsp² square planar, diamagnetic – no d–d transition in the visible region, hence colourless.

questions.q: (a) Explain Werner's theory. (b) Name the types of isomerism in coordination compounds with one example of each.
questions.answer:
(a) Metals show two types of valence: primary (ionisable, equal to the oxidation state) and secondary (non-ionisable, equal to coordination number, directed in space to give geometry such as octahedral); e.g. CoCl3·6NH3 has 3 primary and 6 secondary valences and gives 3 Cl− with AgNO3.
(b) Ionisation – [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br; hydrate – [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 and [Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2·H2O; linkage – nitro and nitrito; coordination – [Co(NH3)6][Cr(CN)6] and [Cr(NH3)6][Co(CN)6]; geometrical – cis/trans-[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]; optical – [Co(en)3]^3+.

questions.q: (a) Explain the geometry and magnetic behaviour of [Ni(CN)4]^2−, [NiCl4]^2− and [Fe(CN)6]^3− using VBT. (b) State two biological importances of complexes.
questions.answer:
(a) [Ni(CN)4]^2−: Ni^2+ d⁸, strong ligand pairs electrons, dsp², square planar, diamagnetic. [NiCl4]^2−: weak ligand, sp³, tetrahedral, two unpaired electrons, paramagnetic. [Fe(CN)6]^3−: Fe^3+ d⁵ with CN−, d²sp³, octahedral, one unpaired electron, paramagnetic.
(b) Chlorophyll (Mg) in photosynthesis and haemoglobin (Fe) in oxygen transport.
